sections.title: Geography
sections.text: Hanoi sits on the Red River Delta in northern Vietnam. Its name, Hà Nội, means "inside the rivers". The city is dotted with lakes, from tiny ponds to the wide West Lake, and Hoàn Kiếm Lake marks the heart of the old town. Unlike the south of the country, Hanoi has four seasons: hot, rainy summers and cool, misty winters.

sections.title: History
sections.text: Emperor Lý Thái Tổ founded the city in 1010 as Thăng Long, "Ascending Dragon", after a legend of a dragon rising from the river. It was the royal capital for most of the next eight centuries, the capital of French Indochina from 1902, and the capital of independent Vietnam after 1945. In 2010 the city celebrated its thousandth birthday.

sections.title: Culture
sections.text: In the Old Quarter, streets still carry the names of the guilds that once worked there, such as Silk Street and Silver Street. Life happens on the pavement: people eat phở and bún chả on low plastic stools and sip egg coffee, a Hanoi invention. Water puppetry (múa rối nước), first performed in the flooded rice fields of the delta, is still staged by Hoàn Kiếm Lake.

etiquette: Cover shoulders and knees at temples, pagodas and the Mausoleum.
Take your shoes off where you see others doing so, for example in homes and some shrines.
Use both hands to give or receive something, especially from an older person.
To cross the street, walk slowly and steadily. Motorbikes will flow around you.

planned.name: Temple of Literature
planned.blurb: A temple to Confucius founded in 1070, and the site of Vietnam's first national university.

timeline.text: Long before any city, rice-farming communities are settling the fertile Red River Delta.
King An Dương Vương builds the spiral citadel of Cổ Loa, just north of today's Hanoi.
The Trưng Sisters lead an uprising against Han Chinese rule. The delta stays under Chinese rule for centuries afterwards.
Under the Tang dynasty the area becomes the seat of the Protectorate of Annan.
Emperor Lý Thái Tổ moves his capital here and names it Thăng Long, "Ascending Dragon".
The Temple of Literature is founded to honour Confucius; it later becomes Vietnam's first national university.
Hồ Quý Ly moves the court south to the new stone citadel of Tây Đô, and Thăng Long becomes Đông Đô, the "Eastern Capital".
At Lunar New Year, Emperor Quang Trung defeats a Qing army at Ngọc Hồi–Đống Đa and retakes Thăng Long.
Emperor Minh Mạng renames the city Hà Nội, "inside the rivers".
France makes northern Vietnam (Tonkin) a protectorate. Hanoi soon gains French boulevards and villas.
Hanoi becomes the capital of French Indochina, and the long Doumer (Long Biên) Bridge opens across the Red River.
On 2 September Ho Chi Minh declares independence on Ba Đình Square.
The Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum opens, and the war ends with the country reunified that spring.
The Đổi Mới reforms open the economy, and Hanoi begins to grow fast.
Hanoi celebrates the thousandth anniversary of Thăng Long.
A busy capital of more than eight million people, still full of lakes, temples and street food.
